state-of-the-art avatar generators (GAGAvatar [22], LivePortrait [23] and HunyuanPortrait [24]), representing up-to-date realistic avatar scenarios. It includes both self- and cross-reenactments, simulating legitimate usage and impersonation attacks.

- Benchmark and Systematic Evaluation: We define a standardized and reproducible benchmark for avatar fingerprinting, including identity-disjoint splits, predefined verification trials, and evaluation protocols. In addition, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of public state-of-the-art avatar fingerprinting systems on our proposed benchmark, evaluating their performance under avatar generator and dataset shift, and also analyzing fairness in terms of gender, ethnicity, and age.
- Exploration of Foundation Models for Avatar Fingerprinting: To the best of our knowledge, we investigate for the first time the use of DINOv2 [25] and CLIP [26] as feature extractors for avatar fingerprinting. Combined with a temporal attention module, we analyze their ability to capture identity-related behavioral cues and compare their performance against state-of-the-art landmark-based approaches.

To date, the number of public databases and benchmarks specifically designed for avatar fingerprinting is very limited. The NVFAIR database introduced by NVIDIA [7] is currently the largest collection of reenacted talkinghead videos, with more than 600,000 videos. NVFAIR comprises scripted and free-form monologues from 46 captured subjects (real data) as well as synthetic reenactments generated with three methods (FaceVid2Vid [13], TPS [14], and LIA [15]), although they are considered old-fashioned nowadays in comparison to state-of-the-art avatar generators, as discussed in Sec. 2.1. In total NVFAIR covers 161 unique identities (by including additional CREMA-D [20] and RAVDESS [21] speakers) with self- and crossreenactments. Access to NVFAIR is restricted via a request form. Also, benchmarking is not possible as the proposed avatar fingerprinting system is not publicly available.

To the best of our knowledge, the only fully public avatar fingerprinting database and benchmark so far is the GAGAvatar-Benchmark [12]. However, it only covers a single talking-head avatar generator (GAGAvatar [22]), limiting diversity in appearance and motion dynamics.

The proposed AVAPrintDB and benchmark is publicly available and covers multiple up-to-date photorealistic avatar generators (GAGAvatar [22], LivePortrait [23] and HunyuanPortrait [24]) and varied source domains (e.g., generator and dataset shift), allowing to evaluate state-of-the-art avatar fingerprinting systems in realistic scenarios.

To intuitively feel the distribution of different numbers of FFPs in the original video frame, Figure 9 shows the comparison between 68 FFPs and 468 FFPs.

The experimental results for the DF(c23) dataset and the Celeb-DF(v2) dataset were obtained by taking the FFPs 68, 118, 168, 218, 268, 318, 368, 418, and 468 using a random function. As shown in the Figure 10, both the ACC and AUC results increase as the number of FFPs increases, but the rate of increase slows down as the number of FFPs continues to increase. However, it is worth noting that the memory consumption also increases as the number of key points increases. For instance, the memory consumption of the 68 FFPs file in each video is 2.65 GB for Celeb-DF(v2) and 0.4 GB for FF,,. On the other hand, the memory consumption of the 468 FFPs file in each video is 18.3 GB for Celeb-DF(v2) and 7.5 GB for DF. After taking into account both model performance and ACC, we concluded that the optimal solution for both DF(c23) dataset and Celeb-DF(v2) dataset is 468 FFPs.

To demonstrate the lightweight nature of the designed ChT classifier, we compared its parameter count with that of other backbone networks, as shown in Table 7, The designed classifier has fewer parameters.

richer and more complex. The original classification of only 68 FFPs of the human face cannot represent the feature difference of the entire face. Therefore, using 468 FFPs of the human face intensively and extracting feature points from the four key parts of the eyes, nose, mouth, and face can expand the difference between true and false faces. For example, the stacking distance of key points displacement of the human face is higher. Furthermore, the ChT model proposed specifically for FFP video frames is also dedicated to face learning and training for each group of frames (60 frames as a group). Our model can learn the fine difference between true and false face videos better than the baseline classification with RNN. Hence, the ACC of the proposed model can be significantly improved on the Celeb-DF(v2) dataset.
